Connect to foundations: The Eddington limit: when light balances gravity ↗ Compare solution assumptions and boundary data in the solution library ↗ 01Isolate a flow without angular momentum Let a mass M be surrounded by gas nearly at rest far away, with specified density ρ∞ and sound speed cs. Assume steady spherical flow, neglect the gas’s self-gravity, angular momentum, and magnetic fields, and first use the isothermal closure P = cs²ρ. Write the inward speed as u > 0. The mass passing through each sphere per unit time is constant. The changing area 4πr² links the increase of speed to the increase of density. Ṁ = 4πr²ρu, d lnρdr = −2r−1ududr 02Eliminate the density gradient Pressure opposes infall. Insert the isothermal relation into momentum balance and use mass conservation to eliminate d lnρ/dr. Although u is positive, its radial derivative is negative for an inflow accelerating toward smaller radius. ududr = −cs²d lnρdr−GMr² (u−cs²u)dudr = 2cs²r−GMr² At u = cs, the coefficient on the left vanishes. A smooth solution with finite slope requires the right-hand side to vanish there too. This regularity selects the sonic point rather than merely identifying a division-by-zero failure. rs = GM2cs², rB ≡ GMcs² = 2rs Some authors include a factor of two in the Bondi radius. Here rB = GM/cs². Do not mix a radius convention from one source with a dimensionless rate coefficient from another. 03Integrate and select the critical branch Use x = r/rs and Mach number 𝓜 = u/cs. Integrate the flow equation and choose the constant so that x = 1 and 𝓜 = 1 coincide. (𝓜−1𝓜)d𝓜dx = 2x−2x² 𝓜²−ln(𝓜²) = 4ln x+4x−3 Bondi inflow from a quiet reservoir joins the subsonic branch at x > 1 to the supersonic branch at x < 1. Expansion at the sonic point gives d𝓜/dx = −1. The opposite slope, +1, belongs to the Parker wind branch. Instead of dividing the ODE across its critical point, the panel bisects the integrated relation. Solving for ln(𝓜²) preserves positive Mach numbers even at small speeds. Substituting each plotted point back into the relation provides a direct residual check. 04Obtain the accretion rate from sonic density Integrating momentum in another form gives an isothermal Bernoulli relation. Set its constant using u → 0 and ρ → ρ∞ at infinity, then evaluate at the sonic point. u²2+cs²ln(ρρ∞)−GMr = 0 ρsρ∞ = e3/2 ṀB = 4πrs²ρscs = 4πλ(GM)²ρ∞cs³, λ = e3/24 ≈ 1.1204 The dimensional estimate rB²ρ∞cs does not determine λ. Its value comes from connecting the outer reservoir through pressure support and sonic regularity. Doubling the density normalization leaves the velocity profile unchanged and doubles the mass flux. 05What changes for a polytropic flow? For P = Kργ with constant K, the local sound speed a² = γP/ρ varies with radius. Combining mass conservation, sonic regularity, and Bernoulli balance yields the following standard relations in terms of the outer sound speed a∞. rs = (5−3γ)GM4a∞², as² = 2a∞²5−3γ λ(γ) = 14[25−3γ](5−3γ)/[2(γ−1)] (1<γ<5/3) The limit γ → 1 recovers the isothermal coefficient; γ → 5/3 gives λ → 1/4. In the latter limit the Newtonian sonic point moves to r = 0, so a formula for a finite regular critical point cannot simply be evaluated there. The panel displays only the isothermal solution. Angular momentum, fields, cooling, radiative feedback, and motion through the gas can alter real accretion. A Bondi rate is not automatically the mass reaching a black hole or the luminosity seen by an observer. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. At fixed outer density, double both the central mass and the outer sound speed. How do Bondi radius and isothermal accretion rate change? Show the answer and reasoning rB ∝ M/cs² halves. The rate scales as M²ρ∞/cs³, giving 4/8 = 1/2. Increased sound speed strengthens pressure support; the isothermal dimensionless coefficient λ stays fixed.
